title: Data Representation
overview: Everything a computer stores is a pattern of bits, so Paper 1 repeatedly asks you to convert between number bases, use binary and decimal prefixes, represent signed integers in two's complement, add and subtract in binary and spot overflow. Questions also test BCD, the uses of hexadecimal and character sets, usually with a short justification of why one representation suits a given use. Most calculation questions award a mark for visible working and a mark for the answer.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of binary magnitudes and the difference between binary prefixes (kibi, mebi, gibi, tebi) and decimal prefixes (kilo, mega, giga, tera).
Understand the different number systems that a computer uses (binary, denary and hexadecimal) and convert integer values between them.
Represent integers in Binary Coded Decimal (BCD), and describe practical applications where BCD and hexadecimal are used.
Represent positive and negative integers using one's complement and two's complement.
Perform binary addition and subtraction using positive and negative integers in two's complement.
Show understanding of how overflow can occur.
Show understanding of and be able to represent character data in its internal binary form, depending on the character set used (ASCII, extended ASCII and Unicode).

definitions.definition: A binary digit, 0 or 1; the smallest unit of data a computer stores.
A group of 8 bits, treated as a single unit of storage. A nibble is 4 bits.
A multiplier based on powers of 2: kibi (Ki, 2^10), mebi (Mi, 2^20), gibi (Gi, 2^30) and tebi (Ti, 2^40).
A multiplier based on powers of 10: kilo (k, 10^3), mega (M, 10^6), giga (G, 10^9) and tera (T, 10^12).
A base-16 number system using the digits 0–9 and A–F; each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits.
A signed representation in which the most significant bit shows the sign (0 = +, 1 = −) and the remaining bits hold the size of the number.
The binary number obtained by inverting every bit (each 0 becomes 1 and each 1 becomes 0).
The one's complement of a binary number plus 1; as a representation, the most significant bit has a negative place value.
When the result of a calculation is too large (or too small) to be stored in the number of bits available.
A representation in which each denary digit is stored separately as a 4-bit binary code (a nibble).
BCD in which two 4-bit digit codes are stored in one byte.
The complete list of characters a computer recognises, each paired with a unique binary code.

sections.title: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
content: Denary (base 10) uses ten digits, binary (base 2) uses 0 and 1, and hexadecimal (base 16) uses 0–9 and A–F. In every base the value comes from place values that increase by a power of the base from the right. For a byte, the binary place values are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. To convert denary to binary, either subtract the largest place values that fit, or divide repeatedly by 2 and read the remainders from the last to the first. To convert between binary and hexadecimal, split the binary into groups of four bits from the right and replace each group with one hex digit; to go from hex to binary, replace each hex digit with its 4-bit pattern. Converting hex to binary first is often the easiest route from hex to denary.
bullets: Hex to denary directly: multiply each digit by its place value (256, 16, 1) and add, e.g. 3F = 3 × 16 + 15 = 63.
Pad the leftmost group to 4 bits before converting to hex, e.g. 101 becomes 0101 = 5.
An n-bit unsigned binary integer can represent 0 to 2^n − 1, so a byte holds 0 to 255 and two bytes hold 0 to 65,535.

examples.label: Denary 202 to binary by repeated division
examples.content:
202 ÷ 2 = 101 remainder 0
101 ÷ 2 = 50 remainder 1
50 ÷ 2 = 25 remainder 0
25 ÷ 2 = 12 remainder 1
12 ÷ 2 = 6 remainder 0
6 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 0
3 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 1
1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1
Read the remainders from the bottom up: 1100 1010
Check: 128 + 64 + 8 + 2 = 202
Hex: 1100 = C, 1010 = A → CA

sections.title: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
content: Decimal prefixes multiply by powers of 10: kilo = 10^3, mega = 10^6, giga = 10^9, tera = 10^12. For many years the computing industry also used 'kilo' to mean 1024 (2^10), which caused confusion: a '1.6 GHz' processor uses the decimal meaning while '8 GB of RAM' usually meant 8 × 2^30 bytes. Binary prefixes were introduced to remove the ambiguity: kibi (KiB) = 2^10, mebi (MiB) = 2^20, gibi (GiB) = 2^30 and tebi (TiB) = 2^40. When presenting a calculated size, choose the prefix that gives one or two digits before the decimal point, and convert all values to the same prefix before combining them.
bullets: Each step up a binary prefix multiplies by 1024; each step up a decimal prefix multiplies by 1000.
The gap grows with size: 1 KiB is 2.4% larger than 1 kB, but 1 TiB is about 10% larger than 1 TB.
Use the prefix named in the question; if it says MiB, divide by 1024 twice, not by 1,000,000.
Storage manufacturers use decimal prefixes, which is why a '500 GB' drive appears as about 465 GiB in an operating system.

examples.label: Converting and presenting sizes
examples.content:
3 MiB = 3 × 1024 × 1024 = 3,145,728 bytes; 3 MB = 3,000,000 bytes.
A file of 45,000 bytes = 45,000 ÷ 1024 ≈ 43.9 KiB.
How many 3.2 MiB files fit on a 4 GiB memory stick?
Convert to the same prefix: 4 GiB = 4 × 1024 = 4096 MiB
4096 ÷ 3.2 = 1280 files

sections.title: Sign and magnitude, one's and two's complement
content: Unsigned integers are stored as plain binary. For signed integers, the simplest idea is sign and magnitude, where the most significant bit (MSB) is the sign; but it has two zeros (+0 and −0) and needs special rules for arithmetic, so computers use two's complement instead. The one's complement of a number is found by inverting every bit; the two's complement is the one's complement plus 1. To store a negative denary number: write the positive value in binary with a leading 0 (fill the byte), invert every bit, then add 1. In two's complement the MSB has a negative place value (−128 in a byte), so 8 bits represent −128 to +127. To read a two's complement value, add the negative MSB value to the positive values of the other 1 bits.
bullets: A leading 1 means the number is negative; a leading 0 means it is zero or positive.
Two's complement has only one zero, and the same adder circuit performs both addition and subtraction.
Quick method: from the right, copy bits up to and including the first 1, then invert every remaining bit.
Taking the two's complement again changes the sign back, e.g. from −44 to +44.
Range of n-bit two's complement: −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1.

examples.label: Quick method and reading a negative value
examples.content:
+44 = 0010 1100
Copy from the right up to and including the first 1: 100
Invert the rest (00101 → 11010): 1101 0100 = −44
Check: −128 + 64 + 16 + 4 = −44

Read 1110 0110: −128 + 64 + 32 + 4 + 2 = −26

examples.label: Sign and magnitude compared with two's complement
examples.content:
+5: sign and magnitude 0000 0101; two's complement 0000 0101
−5: sign and magnitude 1000 0101; two's complement 1111 1011
0: sign and magnitude has 0000 0000 and 1000 0000; two's complement has only 0000 0000

sections.title: Binary addition and subtraction
content: Binary addition works from right to left using four rules: 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 1 = 0 carry 1, and 1 + 1 + 1 = 1 carry 1. Subtraction can be done directly by borrowing (0 − 1 = 1 after borrowing from the next column), but computers subtract by adding the two's complement: A − B = A + (−B). In two's complement arithmetic, any carry out of the most significant bit is discarded.
bullets: Show carries or borrows above the columns; examiners award method marks for visible working.
Convert the answer back to denary to check it.
Discarding the final carry is not the same as overflow; check the signs instead.

examples.label: 14 − 5 by borrowing
examples.content:
1110  (14)
− 0101  (5)
Column 1: 0 − 1 → borrow, 10 − 1 = 1
Column 2: 1 becomes 0 after the borrow; 0 − 0 = 0
Column 3: 1 − 1 = 0
Column 4: 1 − 0 = 1
Result = 1001 = 9

sections.title: Overflow
content: A register has a fixed number of bits, so a result outside the representable range cannot be stored correctly. In two's complement, overflow is shown when two numbers of the same sign are added and the result has the opposite sign: two positives giving a negative, or two negatives giving a positive. The processor records this in the overflow flag of the status register so that software can react.
bullets: Adding numbers of opposite signs can never overflow.
With unsigned numbers, a carry out of the MSB shows the result was too large.
Using more bits (for example 16 instead of 8) widens the range and makes overflow less likely.

examples.label: Two positives giving a negative
examples.content:
0110 0100  (+100)
+ 0011 0010  (+50)
= 1001 0110
The correct answer, +150, is above +127. The MSB is 1, so the result reads as −128 + 16 + 4 + 2 = −106: overflow has occurred.

examples.label: Two negatives giving a positive
examples.content:
1001 1100  (−100)
+ 1100 1110  (−50)
= (1) 0110 1010  (carry out discarded)
The result reads as +106, but the correct answer, −150, is below −128: overflow has occurred.

sections.title: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)
content: BCD stores each denary digit separately in its own nibble, using the codes 0000 (0) to 1001 (9); the codes 1010 to 1111 are never used. Digits can be stored one per byte (leaving four bits unused) or as packed BCD, two digits per byte. BCD is used where denary digits must be displayed or processed individually, such as digital clocks, calculators and seven-segment displays, and for currency, where values such as 0.10 cannot be stored exactly as binary fractions. When two BCD digits are added and the result is above 1001, the processor adds a correction of 0110 so that the digit is valid and a carry passes to the next digit.
bullets: BCD is less storage-efficient than pure binary: 6 of the 16 possible nibble codes are unused.
BCD avoids rounding errors for exact denary values, such as money.
When justifying BCD, link it to each digit being processed or displayed separately.

examples.label: BCD addition with correction: 38 + 47
examples.content:
0011 1000  (38)
+ 0100 0111  (47)
Low digit: 1000 + 0111 = 1111, which is not a valid BCD digit
Add the correction 0110: 1111 + 0110 = 1 0101 → store 0101, carry 1
High digit: 0011 + 0100 + 1 = 1000 (valid)
Result = 1000 0101 = 85

sections.title: Uses of hexadecimal
content: The computer always stores binary; hexadecimal is only a way of writing binary for people. It is shorter and far less error-prone to read, write and remember than long binary strings, yet it converts directly to binary because each hex digit is exactly 4 bits. A 48-bit MAC address, for example, becomes just 12 hex digits.
bullets: Memory addresses and memory dumps when debugging.
MAC addresses, e.g. 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E.
Colour codes in HTML/CSS, e.g. #FF8000 = red FF, green 80, blue 00.
Error codes and machine-code or assembly listings.
URL encoding of special characters, e.g. a space written as %20 (hex 20 = 32, the ASCII code for a space).

sections.title: Character sets
content: Text is stored by giving each character a numeric code from a character set. Standard ASCII uses 7 bits, giving 128 codes covering English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters; it is usually stored in a byte with the MSB set to 0. Extended ASCII uses all 8 bits for 256 codes, adding accented and graphical characters. Unicode can use up to 4 bytes per character, so characters from almost every writing system, plus symbols and emoji, can be represented; its first 128 codes match ASCII.
bullets: Codes are allocated in sequence: 'A' = 65, 'B' = 66; 'a' = 97; the digit '0' = 48, so a lower-case letter is 32 more than its capital.
Because codes are sequential, strings can be sorted and compared by comparing their codes.
Unicode needs more storage per character than ASCII but supports international text in one system.
The character '7' (code 55) is different from the integer 7; converting between them is a common exam point.

formulas.label: Binary prefixes
formulas.expression: 1 KiB = 2^10 bytes; 1 MiB = 2^20 bytes; 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes; 1 TiB = 2^40 bytes

formulas.label: Decimal prefixes
formulas.expression: 1 kB = 10^3 bytes; 1 MB = 10^6 bytes; 1 GB = 10^9 bytes; 1 TB = 10^12 bytes

formulas.label: BCD addition correction
formulas.expression: if a digit sum > 1001, add 0110 and carry 1 to the next digit

comparisonTable.title: Choosing a representation
rows: Counts and addresses that are never negative
Two zeros; arithmetic needs special rules
Signed integer arithmetic in the ALU
Range is limited and overflow can occur
Displaying binary to humans (addresses, colours, MAC addresses)
Only a notation: the computer still stores binary
Digit displays and exact currency values
Wastes storage: 6 of 16 nibble codes are unused
Uses more bytes per character than ASCII

analysisChains.title: Increasing the number of bits in a register
steps: Each extra bit doubles the number of values that can be represented
The two's complement range widens, e.g. 8 bits (−128 to 127) to 16 bits (−32,768 to 32,767)
Calculations are less likely to overflow
But each value needs more memory and wider buses to move
analysisChains.evaluation: Choose the smallest word size that safely covers the expected range of values; a sensor reading 0–200 fits a byte, but a bank balance does not.

analysisChains.title: Storing a price in BCD rather than pure binary
steps: Each denary digit is stored exactly in its own nibble
No binary fraction approximation is needed for values such as 0.10
Rounding errors in financial totals are avoided
But more bits are needed and addition needs a correction step
analysisChains.evaluation: BCD is justified where exact denary values or digit-by-digit display matter; for general calculation, pure binary is more compact and faster.

analysisChains.title: Moving from ASCII to Unicode
steps: Characters from many alphabets can be represented
Software can be used internationally with one encoding
Each character may need 2–4 bytes instead of 1
Files and transmissions containing plain English text become larger
analysisChains.evaluation: For a system used only with English text, ASCII is sufficient and smaller; for any multilingual or web application, Unicode is necessary.

examTips: Show your working for every conversion (column headings, division remainders or the invert-and-add-1 steps); calculation questions usually give one mark for working and one for the answer.
Always check two's complement answers by converting back to denary using −128 as the MSB value.
Do not confuse one's complement (invert the bits) with two's complement (invert, then add 1).
When asked to identify overflow, state the correct denary answer and why it is outside the representable range.
Read the prefix carefully: KiB/MiB/GiB use 1024, kB/MB/GB use 1000.
For 'justify the use of BCD/hex' questions, name a specific application and the feature that makes the representation suitable.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to add 1 after inverting the bits when forming a two's complement negative.
Forgetting the leading 0 on the positive value before taking the two's complement.
Treating a discarded final carry as overflow instead of checking whether the sign of the result is valid.
Converting a whole number to BCD as if it were pure binary, instead of converting each digit separately.
Using 1000 instead of 1024 for kibi/mebi prefixes (or the reverse).
Writing hex digits above 9 as numbers, e.g. writing '11' instead of 'B'.
Saying extended ASCII is Unicode; extended ASCII is still limited to 256 characters.

quickRecall.question: How many bytes are in 1 KiB and in 1 kB?
What is the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer?
How do you find the two's complement of a negative number?
quickRecall.answer: Write the positive value in binary with a leading 0, invert every bit, then add 1.

quickRecall.question: Why is two's complement preferred to sign and magnitude?
quickRecall.answer: It has only one zero, and addition and subtraction use the same simple adder with no special rules.

quickRecall.question: How is overflow detected when adding two's complement numbers?
quickRecall.answer: Two numbers of the same sign are added and the result has the opposite sign.

quickRecall.question: What is 0011 1001 in BCD?
quickRecall.answer: 39 — each nibble is one denary digit (3 and 9).

quickRecall.question: What is packed BCD?
quickRecall.answer: BCD with two digit codes stored in one byte.

quickRecall.question: Give two uses of hexadecimal.
quickRecall.answer: Any two of: memory addresses, MAC addresses, HTML colour codes, error codes, machine-code/assembly listings, URL encoding.

quickRecall.question: Why is Unicode needed when ASCII exists?
quickRecall.answer: ASCII has only 128 (or 256 extended) codes, which cannot represent characters from all languages; Unicode can.
